extracted.intended_audience: early-career researchers and academics applying for research funding (especially university-based applicants)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for researchers on responding to grant/fellowship rejections: emotional framing, reviewing feedback, adjusting project scale and timing, building a funding portfolio, and using networks to improve future success. Advice is oriented to career development and institutional expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normalize and depersonalise rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Step one to handling rejections is to a) normalise them and b) depersonalise them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge emotional responses (sadness, anger, frustration). Recognise that rejection is common (success rates for top schemes range from 1% to under 20%) and does not mean your idea is worthless. Be aware that the stakes differ by employment security (precarious contracts make rejections harder).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect to be unsuccessful on first attempt
rubrics_metrics.description: Expect to be unsuccessful on first attempt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build anticipated rejection into project planning and research strategy so you can iterate and keep momentum rather than stopping after an early rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know your institutional expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Familiarise yourself with the institutional and departmental agenda and plans (e.g., Research Excellence Framework) to understand available support and how to shape your strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify structures of support (line manager, head of subject, local and wider university research office, trusted critical friends). Use institutional knowledge to align projects with internal priorities and resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand expectations regarding your funding profile for recruitment and promotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand what funding profile is expected for recruitment into academic roles and for promotion in your institutional and international context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn the funding ecosystem, policies, processes, and procedures specific to your context so you can plan which schemes to target and when.

rubrics_metrics.name: Share your unsuccessful stories (transparency on CV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be transparent about unsuccessful funding applications as indicators of ambition, effort, resilience, and vision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicate on your CV being placed on reserve lists or having repurposed a larger proposal into a pilot; this signals learning and commitment. Use storytelling/visibility (e.g., videos or posts) to normalise rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify obstacles by reflecting on reviewer feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Take time to reflect on the feedback you received and identify obstacles to funding success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't treat rejection as failure; recognise that feedback can be disheartening or misaligned (e.g., a reviewer pushing their own agenda). Use your support network to interpret feedback and plan next steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break large projects into smaller pilots/proof-of-concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Depending on the scale of the proposed project, there may be value in breaking it into smaller chunks and starting with a pilot or 'proof of concept' first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use smaller awards to generate preliminary data, strengthen the case for larger grants, and demonstrate feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop a funding portfolio and build incrementally
rubrics_metrics.description: Build up to big projects brick by brick by breaking ideas into small, medium, and large scales and being clear about interdependencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show a long-term vision through an incremental funding strategy; use workshops and institutional support to develop your funding profile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t underestimate timing
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an element of luck and serendipity: a fundable idea can arrive at the wrong time and vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of wider social and political agendas and how particular schemes align with them; consider whether timing (e.g., anniversaries, events) can be used intentionally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control the controllables: craft a compelling narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: While some things are beyond your control (e.g., who sits on the panel), you can control how you tell the story of why your idea matters and why it matters now.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refine the case for significance and timeliness; align language and framing with funder priorities and current events where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create visibility for new or challenging ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare the ground for cutting-edge or methodologically novel ideas by creating visibility through targeted publications and other dissemination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PhD or disruptive projects may meet community reluctance; use papers, talks, and outreach to make ideas familiar and easier for reviewers to accept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have a strong personal and professional network
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong network is crucial when feedback is contradictory or absent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After the initial emotional reaction, seek diverse feedback: share your application and the scheme's evaluation criteria with critical friends and ask why they would or would not fund the project.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have a diverse support network and be selective about advice
rubrics_metrics.description: Diversity of interlocutors matters because different people will give different guidance (e.g., 'you're not ready' vs 'go for it').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflect on who you listen to; balance mentors, supervisors, colleagues, and critical friends to regain perspective and make informed decisions about next steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repurpose intellectual work from unsuccessful applications
rubrics_metrics.description: An unfunded application still represents intellectual work that can be repurposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use outcomes of the application process to produce review/position papers, publications, new collaborations, reworked projects, or pilot studies — all of which can lead to future funding success.
